articles.title: Woman raped by strangers after being drugged by husband calls for consent law changes
articles.summary:
Four men convicted of sexual assault and rape of Joanne Young, whose husband advertised her on swinging websites

•

blocks.text: A woman who was raped by strangers after being drugged by her husband has warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”, as four men who abused her were convicted on Thursday.

Philip Young, 50, advertised his then wife, Joanne Young, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” in which anything could be done to her by those who answered the adverts, jurors were told.
The former Conservative councillor pleaded guilty earlier in the year to dozens of charges of abuse against his former wife, who has waived her right to anonymity.
On Thursday, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32; Richard Wilkins, 62; Norman Macksoni, 48; and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were convicted of various offences against Joanne Young after a three-week trial.

The case has drawn comparisons to that of Gisèle Pelicot, who was drugged by her husband and raped by dozens of strangers in France. It can now be revealed that Wiltshire police received advice from the Pelicot investigators on how to approach their inquiries.
The Crown Prosecution Service said it was the first time a jury had convicted multiple defendants relating to organised drug-facilitated sexual assault in England.
After the verdicts, Wiltshire police said that although rare, the true scale of drug-facilitated sexual offences in the UK could be significantly underreported.

In a statement outside court, Joanne Young – whose bravery was praised by the judge – said the convictions meant “that those who find themselves facing what I have are more likely to come forward, and more likely to have faith in the criminal justice system”.

Saying that she now lives “with a pain that’s hard to put into words”, she added: “Consent has to come from the person themselves. No one should be able to give it on your behalf, and no one should be able to rely on someone else’s word that you agreed.
“At no point did anyone ask me for my consent. I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in the future.”

Sanderson-Doyle, a Ministry of Defence contractor from Swindon, was convicted of sexual assault and assault by penetration; Wilkins, a taxi driver from Swindon, was found guilty of assault by penetration and rape; Macksoni, a former DJ and waste management worker from Bedfordshire, was convicted of rape; and Hassan, also from Swindon, was found guilty of sexual assault.
A further defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, from Somerset, has admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.
A spokesperson for Wiltshire police, which investigated Young’s offending, said other victims in similar cases may not know they had been targeted.

He added: “While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly underreported crime type.

“Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption. These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging.”
Joanne said the abuse had a devastating impact on her life and the lives of her children but she hoped the verdict would give other victims of abuse the confidence to come forward.

“The court has today shown that there will be consequences for those who make the choice to abuse,” she said. “I’m determined that their choices will not define me, and I will now use my experience to try to help others. I also owe it to myself to live the best life I can with my children and loved ones as we move forward.”

blocks.caption: Joanne Young. Photograph: Jack Taylor/Reuters

blocks.text: Mr Justice Saini refused bail applications for the four men convicted on Thursday, telling them they all faced “significant custodial sentences”.
All of the men, including Young and Hamilton, will be sentenced on 21 and 22 December at Winchester crown court.

Young, a father of three, pleaded guilty in January to a total of 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife. He also admitted three charges of making indecent images of children, one of possessing prohibited images of children in July 2024 and four counts of possessing an extreme pornographic image between January 2019 and January 2024.

Over more than a decade, Young – who served as a Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 – drugged and raped his wife and invited other men on websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and FabSwingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.
Prosecutors told the court the case was about whether it was ever reasonable to have sex with an unknown woman without checking with her first.

Sanderson-Doyle responded to an online advert in 2015 and visited the couple’s home in June 2016. Young filmed him sexually assaulting Joanne as she was drugged, blindfolded and restrained, and heard saying “No”.

Wilkins went to the home in July 2016. Young filmed Wilkins abusing Joanne who again was blindfolded, restrained and seemingly asleep, without obtaining her consent. Police footage of his arrest shows the officers identifying him through distinctive tattoos.

Macksoni visited and raped Joanne in February 2017, while Hassan sexually assaulted her in February 2023. Messages and digital evidence showed Young arranged for Hassan to visit and Hassan had sexual contact with her while she believed he was her husband.

Speaking after the verdicts, James Foster, a specialist prosecutor at the CPS, said: “These men chose to commit unspeakable acts of abuse against Joanne Young without bothering to check if she was consenting.

“By building the case with a suspect-centric approach, we could prove to a jury that Philip Young could not provide consent on the victim’s behalf and each defendant played a part in this horrific sexual abuse.

“During the trial, Macksoni, Wilkins, Sanderson-Doyle and Hassan hid behind the claim that they believed she was freely entering into a sexual relationship with them, despite never seeking reassurances that this was in fact the case.”

articles.title: Spuds in space: scientists say potatoes could be key food source for future moon base
articles.summary:
New report finds that potatoes should be able to grow on moon after they were successfully cultivated in simulated lunar soil

The humble potato could be the key to sustaining human life on…

blocks.text: The humble potato could be the key to sustaining human life on the moon, according to a new scientific report asserting that prolonged lunar exploration will depend on life support systems capable of producing food there.
Potatoes are an ideal candidate for farming on the moon, scientists on a project backed by the US space agency Nasa concluded, after they succeeded in growing them in simulated lunar soil.

The authors of the resulting US study produced a report titled “Growth and molecular responses of potato to lunar regolith simulants”, published in the journal npj Microgravity, with regolith referring to the kind of blanket of loose stones and dust covering solid rock that is found on the surface of the moon, Mars, asteroids and parts of Earth.

“Potatoes provide more calories per land area than many other crops,” said Oregon State University plant biologist Aymeric Goyer, who led the study. “They are nutritious – ​they provide more potassium than a banana, are rich in vitamin C, have good proteins – and they have a high satiety index.”

The experiment envisions lunar greenhouses in the future. The scientists were able to grow viable potatoes that are safe to eat, emphasizing that “it is essential to ensure that the food produced is edible”.

The researchers used “lunar regolith simulants”, or engineered, Earth-based materials to replicate the properties of moon dust and soil, adding varying levels of vermicompost, an organic soil amendment made when composting worms – typically red wigglers (Eisenia fetida) – break down food scraps and organic waste, to conduct the experiments.

The study involved the modoc potato, an early-maturing cultivar with ⁠reddish skin and white flesh. The report comes as both the US and China have announced plans to establish long-term or permanent bases near the lunar south pole. Nasa hopes to return astronauts to the moon’s surface in 2028, while China aims for the same before 2030. Long-term bases may follow and probably could not be supplied with all its food needs from the Earth alone.

Goyer said that lunar regolith of dust and rock “does not contain any nitrogen, so no crop would grow without supplementing it”, and potatoes planted in lunar material without vermicompost produced almost no roots or tubers.

Potatoes grown with as little as 5% vermicompost, however, grew some roots and tubers. But at 30% vermicompost, the yield was identical to potatoes grown under the same conditions in the Earth’s soil.

Goyer acknowledged that researchers had tested but had not yet tasted the sample potatoes, which were grown in small pots and yielded potatoes of less than a third of an ounce (10 grams), even in Earth soil. “We used what we harvested for lab analyses,” he said.
A second study, he said, used larger pots in which researchers “obtained potatoes of size you typically see at the store”.

A 2017 study at the International Potato Center in Peru, where potatoes originated as a tuber native to the Andes, concluded that the plant could sprout on Mars. The study used a potato tube in a container that mimics Martian temperatures and atmospheric conditions.

Earlier this year, Nasa astronaut Don Pettit showed off a potato named “Spudnik” he had grown in the bottom half of a plastic containment bag in space. In the microgravity environment of the International Space Station, Space.com noted, the purple potato’s sprouts grew straight up into the air.

“In the weightlessness of orbit, roots generally head towards moisture but sometimes they get confused and grow ‘upwards’,” Pettit wrote. The astronaut acknowledged a debt to The Martian feature film in which a marooned astronaut played by Matt Damon figures out a way to grow and live off of potatoes.
after newsletter promotion
The latest study noted that lunar regolith alone is hostile to crops due to its heavy metal content.

“Without organic matter, potatoes take up too much heavy metals, which can become toxic for the plants. Organic matter helps make heavy metals less available to the plants, so plants do not over-accumulate them,” Goyer said.
But potatoes are not the only contender for a crop that can can be grown on the moon. A study published in March documented chickpeas grown in lunar regolith supplemented with vermicompost.
“People are also working with tomatoes, lettuce ​and legumes like alfalfa,” Goyer said.
Oregon State space biologist and study co-author David Handy said what can be grown on the moon could also benefit life on Earth.

“The technologies that are invented as a result can be used to ​produce food in regions of low agricultural ‌output that are reliant on shipments, ​such as inner cities and desert communities,” Handy said, adding that continued research using lunar-type soil “will lead to techniques that can be used to improve soil quality, as well as remediate contaminated soils to improve sustainable agriculture here”.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

blocks.text: US special envoy Jared Kushner said unity in Europe was clear in the talks and that support for Ukraine remained strong.
"What we came away from today with is really seeing that Europe is very united and very, very strong in their support of Ukraine," Kushner said. "We relayed this to President Trump."
Kushner said this would also be relayed to the Russian delegation and that there was "a real desire for peace."
Kushner said that Trump had joined the Berlin meeting by phone and provided an update on the talks in Shenzhen with President Putin and President Xi.
"He sent a very strong message to both of them on the desire for peace and would like to engage with both of them very aggressively to get there," Kushner said.

Kushner told reporters the talks with European leaders ⁠and ​Ukrainian President ​Volodymyr Zelenskyy had "made a lot ​of progress ‌on what those security ​guarantees ⁠can look like," as well ⁠as ​a post-war prosperity plan.

articles.title: Call for police to investigate Scottish hospital after 19 deaths due to surgery
articles.summary:
Surgeon at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary says he repeatedly voiced concerns that patients may have died unnecessarily

A senior surgeon has called for a criminal investigation into a Scottish…

blocks.text: A senior surgeon has called for a criminal investigation into a Scottish hospital after it emerged that at least 19 patients had died from avoidable complications due to surgery.

Dr Mohammed Habib, a consultant at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, said he had repeatedly reported concerns about the hospital’s liver and pancreatic surgery from 2021 onwards and believed dozens of patients may have died unnecessarily there.

Calling for a police investigation into corporate homicide at the hospital, Habib alleged that senior officials at NHS Grampian, the crisis-hit health board which runs it, failed to take the correct action quickly enough.

blocks.caption: Dr Mohammed Habib. Photograph: PA

blocks.text: Habib said NHS Grampian eventually commissioned an expert report to investigate his allegations, and those from a second whistleblower, which confirmed his allegations that 19 patients had died due to “serious adverse events” caused by surgery between 2015 and 2021.
Their internal report was published on Thursday by Habib’s solicitor, Aamer Anwar.

Habib’s comments and the findings were discussed in Holyrood later on Thursday. John Swinney, Scotland’s first minister, said Habib’s disclosures were “of the gravest concern”. The NHS had legal duties to give patients the best possible care and to quickly investigate allegations about safety failures, he said.
But he rebuffed demands from Michael Marra, the Scottish Labour leader, for a criminal investigation into the “systemic failures” at NHS Grampian.
Speaking at first minister’s questions, Marra said the families of the 19 people who died “deserve answers and deserve justice.”

Swinney denied that the government had ignored Habib’s complaints and said the recent decision to demand changes of leadership and urgent reforms at the board should produce the necessary improvements.

Laura Skaife-Knight, chief executive of NHS Grampian, said: “We are aware of the serious allegations raised today. A thorough investigation has already taken place into these matters, with some elements of that work ongoing. Any new evidence or information will be carefully considered, and NHS Grampian will continue to respond through the appropriate clinical, governance and legal processes.

“We understand the allegations will cause further concern to patients, members of the public and staff. It is important we respect patient and employee confidentiality, but we can highlight that where reviews identify issues around patient care, the appropriate duty of candour processes are followed. This includes direct communication with patients and families where required.
“If our consideration of any new evidence identifies further individuals who should be contacted, we will do so. Patient safety remains our highest priority.”

The two external experts who carried out the review in 2022, surgery professors at Edinburgh and Leeds universities, concluded the “extremely high” death rate at Aberdeen between 2017 and 2020 ran as high as 18% within liver and pancreatic surgery.
It said the national average for surgery-related fatalities was 2-3% for that speciality, depending on the patient’s condition.

The surgeon, who still works at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, said the unit continued operating on patients. He then flagged the cases of four other patients who had died during or after surgery since that expert report was completed.

In March 2026, another external expert said it was imperative that surgery ended there, telling hospital executives its “persistent high mortality in complex surgery is a red-flag indicator of systemic failure”. The liver and pancreatic surgery department was then shut down.
Based on the fatality calculations made in 2022, Habib said dozens of patients may have died unnecessarily at the hospital.
He said he had repeatedly contacted the police, Scottish government ministers and Scotland’s independent whistleblowing officer, but was fobbed off, or told the cases he raised were time-barred.

His allegations are the latest in a series of medical and managerial crises at NHS Grampian, which has led to paediatric surgery at Gray’s hospital being shut down, the replacement of the board’s chairperson and its medical director, and independent investigations into other serious adverse events at its hospitals.
Last week, Angela Constance, the Scottish health secretary, told MSPs there were extremely serious systemic problems with mismanagement and underperformance at NHS Grampian.
In a statement at Holyrood, she told MSPs the health board faced being put into special measures if its current reforms were not introduced quickly or effectively enough.

Last week, a report by Healthcare Improvement Scotland (HIS), an NHS watchdog, found “very serious shortcomings with NHS Grampian’s leadership”, which included failing to be transparent and accurate in its accounts of its actions.
There had been “persistent, serious concerns about safety, quality, clinical governance and leadership” at the board, it said.
However, the HIS report only identified one patient death due to a serious adverse event.

Habib and Anwar said the evidence from the expert review into Habib’s unit had shown many more deaths were avoidable, and that this raised their concerns about whether the full extent of the crisis at NHS Grampian was being covered up.
Habib said NHS Grampian is “avoiding accountability by not being transparent about what damage has been done, while promising heaven and earth going forward.
“In every other death at the hands of the state, families would be entitled to understand the circumstances of their loved ones’ death. [They] deserve to know how and why their loved one died.”

Anwar said the Lord Advocate, Ruth Charteris KC, should instruct her lawyers and Police Scotland to launch a criminal investigation. Ministers should immediately place NHS Grampian into special measures, he added.

There was a “catastrophic failure to act” at NHS Grampian, Anwar said. “While the Grampian leadership was busy burying evidence behind complex medical jargon, they also failed to explain to bereaved families that their loved ones had died after the wrong operation.”

A Scottish government spokesperson said: “We recognise the courage shown by this whistleblower to raise concerns. Everyone who works in our NHS should feel safe and supported to speak up without fear of detriment.
“Ministers have already committed to transparently setting out all engagement with NHS Grampian in relation to the concerns raised in the HIS Review.

“The government took action and repeatedly raised the concerns of Dr Habib with both Healthcare Improvement Scotland and NHS Grampian. As the HIS review set out last week, there were clear failures in the former medical leadership and in how concerns were being addressed within NHS Grampian.
“NHS Grampian is now subject to a very significant level of intervention and an unprecedented level of support.
“Any criminal investigation is a matter for Police Scotland.”
Police Scotland has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Victim's lawyers back closed testimony, stronger protection for Duterte ICC trial witnesses
articles.summary: PRAGUE, Czech Republic - Amid the “exceptional circumstances” in former President Rodrigo Duterte"s International Criminal Court (ICC) case, closed sessions and stronger protections for testifying…
articles.byline: Andy Peñafuerte III, Jay-vee Marasigan Pangan

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 1:56am

PRAGUE, Czech Republic – Amid the “exceptional circumstances” in former President Rodrigo Duterte’s International Criminal Court (ICC) case, closed sessions and stronger protections for testifying witnesses are necessary, the victims’ lawyers tell the Trial Chamber III.

While Common Legal Representatives of the Victims (CLRV) Gilbert Andres, Joel Butuyan, and Paolina Massidda back the Office of the Prosecutor’s request for in-court protective measures for victims and witnesses, they suggest the court adopt a “comprehensive and prospective approach” in its assessment.

In particular, the lawyers request the use of closed sessions “for all the testimony” of most witnesses, combined with pseudonyms and voice distortions for “effective protection,” given the “objectively justifiable risks” these individuals face.

“The pseudonym would prevent the formal identification of the witness in the proceedings, while closed session testimony would prevent the disclosure of the substantive and contextual details capable of revealing [REDACTED] identity,” the lawyers argued in their filing released on November 19.
Political and social context

The prosecution had earlier sought protective and special measures for 55 witnesses expected to testify in Duterte’s trial, including pseudonyms, face and voice distortion, private or closed sessions, and psychological support for some witnesses.

The victims’ lawyers said public hearings remain a fundamental principle at the ICC, but that openness must be balanced against the Court’s obligation to protect the safety, physical and psychological well-being, dignity and privacy of victims and witnesses.

Noting the “particular political and social context” of Duterte’s case, the CLRVs said conventional protective measures “do not necessarily eliminate the risk of identification,” particularly when details disclosed during testimony could reveal a witness’s identity.

The CLRVs also urged judges to consider risks to witnesses’ families, saying that in the Philippines’ “close-knit communities and family-oriented social context”, the consequences of identifying a witness could extend beyond the person testifying.

In another redacted section, the lawyers said public identification in the “prevailing political and social climate in the Philippines” could expose a witness to a “real risk of harm, intimidation and/or social ostracism.”
“Accordingly, in adjudicating the Request, the Chamber should consider not only the risks faced by the witness, but also the foreseeable repercussions [REDACTED] family.”
Participating victims and witnesses
The ICC’s page on Duterte’s case states that Trial Chamber III has authorized more than 500 victims to participate in the proceedings set to open on November 30.
“More victims may apply and be authorised to participate in the trial,” the page stated.
Victims and witnesses have different roles in ICC proceedings.

“Witnesses give evidence in Court to help establish the facts of a case. They may be eyewitnesses, people with inside knowledge, or experts. Victims could also be witnesses or be authorized by the judges to appear and present their own views before the Court.

Participating victims have suffered harm from crimes related to the case and have been granted the right to participate by the judges. Participating victims are represented by their own representative/lawyer in the courtroom, who represents their views and concerns.”

The ICC said its obligation to protect the safety, physical and psychological well-being, dignity and privacy of victims and witnesses starts from the investigation and continues throughout the proceedings.
“Intimidating or interfering with witnesses at any stage of the investigations or the proceedings can constitute an offence against the administration of justice at the ICC.”
The ICC also reminds the public that the identities of protected witnesses remain confidential and must be respected.
“Respecting witnesses means respecting the justice process.” — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Jimmy Dimly is back and we should treasure him while we can | John Crace
articles.summary: Old-school Tory with a heart wants to make London fun again – just don’t mention Brexit

blocks.text: Sooner or later, Sadiq Khan’s luck was bound to run out. Or was it? When he first stood for London mayor in 2016, the Tory candidate was Zac Goldsmith, who was accused of running a racist campaign. Not the brightest move in one of the most multicultural cities in Europe. Not to be outdone, four years later the Conservatives chose the completely anonymous Shaun Bailey. Even Shaun wasn’t sure who Shaun was. Especially when he was quite sure he could have sworn he wasn’t the Shaun Bailey who had an apparent Christmas party during lockdown, which he said “turned into something once I left”.

As if to prove it wasn’t an accident that they had previously fielded the worst candidates possible, the Tories came up with Susan Hall in 2024. A politician who makes Liz Truss look accomplished. Her campaign was one of the most joyous imaginable. A wild ride of one idiotic speech to the next. You kept thinking the Conservatives must be having a laugh and would unveil their serious candidate. Only they never did. The only votes she got were from those who had never heard her speak. The Tories would have done better if they had put up a turnip.

This time, the Tories are determined to take themselves a little more seriously. With the emphasis on a little. Enter James Cleverly. One of this column’s favourite sons. It’s only with his reappearance that you realise quite how much you’ve missed him. James has the CV of a political heavyweight. But at heart he still is, and always will be, Jimmy Dimly. The foreign secretary who rubbished Rishi Sunak’s Rwanda plan as “bat-shit crazy” only to find himself moved sideways to home secretary where he was forced to defend and implement it.

blocks.caption: Cleverly with his wife, Susie. Disaster follows him around like an ultra-needy cockapoo. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA

blocks.text: Things like this keep happening to Jimmy D. Disaster follows him around like an ultra-needy cockapoo. Yet you can’t help loving him for it. Because there’s something rather sweet about a man who takes himself quite so seriously. Never realising that the joke’s on him. People are laughing at him, not with him. A man who always seems to be living his life several sentences behind every conversation. Stuck in second gear. Someone who means well, but can’t quite keep up. We don’t know yet if Sadiq is planning to stand for a fourth term in 2028, but he may be looking at Dimly and thinking things could have been a lot worse.

Inside a central London office suite on Thursday morning, Jimmy D and the two other Tory mayoral candidates, Festus Akinbusoye and Sara Gezdari, gathered to hear the results of the first round of voting. Or only round. The returning officer announced that Dimly had received 86% of the vote and was duly elected. Interestingly, we weren’t told how many people had voted. I guess it’s less embarrassing than saying Jimmy had received 43 votes. Fair to say that this is not an election that has gripped the Tory party. Nor London. No one is much interested in who is going to be runner-up again to Labour.

Jimmy D gave a big smile. This was his moment and he was going to milk it. He strode to the lectern to address a largely uninterested audience. First, he wanted to thank Festus and Sara for the brilliant campaigns they had run and for the lively conversations they had sparked. “You are an asset to London and the whole country,” he said. Er … hang on a mo. What campaigns and what conversations? This was the first time most of London had heard of Festus and Sara, so it was tragic that the acclaim was for their imminent return to obscurity.

“Nobody loves London more than me,” Dimly continued. So he wasn’t planning to stand again as an MP. He was all in for London. This sounded more like a man clinging to a life raft than an endorsement of the capital. In truth, he has always looked out of sorts in Kemi Badenoch’s Reform-lite Conservative party. He had been more of an old-school Tory who was never comfortable just trashing foreigners and people on benefits. So this was more a last chance of extending his political career while maintaining some self-respect rather than a statement of commitment. He might be a bit crap, but he was a bit crap with a heart.

We then got five minutes of a love letter to London. “The answer to ‘why London’ is because London is London,” he said gnomically. At times like these, Dimly excels himself. We should treasure him while we still have him. London was the best city in the world. Then, as if realising he had just given a party broadcast on behalf of Sadiq, he gave us five minutes on why London was the most rubbish city in the world.

Basically everything that was wrong with London was the fault of “Khan”. Jimmy couldn’t bring himself to use his first name. Everywhere you went there were people being murdered in front of your eyes and motorists had been deprived of the opportunity of driving at high speed and killing cyclists and pedestrians. Only Dimly could make London a fun place again. To all those people who had been up all night playing Grand Theft Auto VI, he was going to turn the capital into a video game. London was going to be bigger than big. So big no one would ever miss it again. Or something.

There was just time for a few questions. How did he feel about having supported Truss’s mini-budget and being pro-Brexit? On the whole, Londoners weren’t that keen on either of these. Two-thirds of Londoners reckoned Brexit had been a disaster. How was he going to reconcile that one? Now Jimmy D struggled with his hearing. Turned out he couldn’t make out the Brexit word.
after newsletter promotion

He didn’t want to talk about the past, he was the future. Except when he was talking about the Wrath of Khan. “Khan hates London,” he insisted. “What’s more Andy Burnham hates London too.” In the DimlyVerse, neither Sadiq nor Andy would be happy until the capital had been razed to the ground.

What about the commitment to abandoning net zero and membership of the ECHR? Those were Kemi’s red lines. Were they his? Jimmy shuffled awkwardly and mumbled “Yes”. A lie. Dimly believes in both. As do most Londoners. There has almost certainly been a pact that Kemi will look the other way so long as Jimmy doesn’t make a big deal about the differences in their politics.

Dimly just wanted to re-emphasise his commitment to London. He was all for the things that Londoners wanted. And if he wasn’t, he would do his best to pretend that he was. He couldn’t say fairer than that. “I am only going to comment on my comments,” he said in conclusion. Sometimes, it’s hard not to love him. At the very least, the next two years will be a golden time for sketch writers.

articles.title: Marcos seeks action on illegal, unregulated fishing at APEC
articles.summary: SHENZHEN - President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. raised the matter of illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing during the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 1:53am
SHENZHEN – President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. raised the matter of illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing during the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting.
The Philippine leader sought concerted action against questionable fishing practices, according to the Presidential Communications Office (PCO).
Marcos likewise pushed for the digital transformation of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) through artificial intelligence and a charter for a sustainable blue economy,

The president also reaffirmed the Philippines' support for the rules-based multilateral trading system and highlighted the conclusion of the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement under the country’s chairship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2026.

He said that APEC discussions “must translate into real benefits for the people” through job creation, better access to healthcare, and preparation for demographic change and a growing silver economy.
Chile
Also on Thursday, the Philippines and Chile on Thursday formally signed their Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA).
The signing was led by Marcos and Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast during a bilateral meeting held at the Shenzhen International Exchange Center.
Marcos said the signing of the free trade deal was something that the Philippines "very much hoped for."
"We're very happy that we have finally come to a formal agreement," the Philippine President said.

"The FTA is going to provide us with a very, very important foundation to build on to make this trade, this relationship, not only in trade, not only between governments, but between our people—stronger, more vibrant, and deeper," he added.
Peru
Marcos and Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori also on Thursday discussed the possibility of establishing a joint trade commission to advance bilateral trade.

The PCO said that Marcos and Fujimori also talked about exploring cooperation in environmental protection and disaster risk reduction and management amid the threat of a super El Niño that is expected to affect both countries.

During the bilateral meeting, the two leaders also reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening bilateral ties and advancing cooperation in areas of mutual interest. –Giselle Ombay/NB, GMA News

articles.title: Xi-Trump-Putin summit: What did it achieve?
articles.summary: The presidents of China, the US and Russia have held an unprecedented summit. While Trump said the three leaders were "making history," Xi described the talks as "fruitful," and Putin called them…

image.caption: The 'peace declaration' released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in IranImage: Doug Mills/The New York Times/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, bringing together the leaders of the world's three most powerful military powers amid heightened geopolitical tensions.
Xi hailed the talks as "groundbreaking," saying discussions ranged from global governance and denuclearization to the war in Ukraine and energy security.
The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in Iran.

Instead, the three leaders agreed to pursue reforms of the United Nations, limit the role of the International Criminal Court and reaffirm their commitment to avoiding nuclear war. They also pledged to boost supplies of refined petroleum products to address global energy challenges.
The tightly choreographed meeting fueled concerns that Beijing, Washington and Moscow could seek to reshape the international order around competing spheres of influence.
While Xi said the talks with Trump and Putin were "positive, constructive and fruitful," Trump heralded the gathering as "really making history."
Leaders of China, Russia, US praised trilateral summit as 'success'
Who gained the most from the meeting?

For Putin, the three-way talks, and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier, offered a chance to show the world that he was on par with the leaders of the US and China despite Western efforts to isolate him since he launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Emma Chanlett-Avery, senior director for Political-Security Affairs at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), said Putin had the most to gain from the meeting as "he appeared on the world stage as one of the dominant players in the world."
Chim Lee, a senior analyst with The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), echoed this view.
The meeting itself is a "major outcome for Russia," he told DW, pointing to Russian media coverage that has cast it as "reinforcing Russia's standing in the world."
Beijing reluctant to accept nuclear limits
The joint statement also said the leaders are committed to work to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February.
Trump has said he wants "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China.
But Beijing has so far been reluctant to accept limits as its estimated arsenal of around 500 warheads remains far smaller than those of Russia and the US.
Moscow and Washington are believed to possess more than 5,000 warheads each.
Why China is surging its nuclear forces

Lee said China is unlikely to participate in a trilateral institutionalized setting to control nuclear arms. "The gap between China's nuclear arsenal and those of Russia and US is still quite large. From China's perspective, it doesn't seem to make a lot of sense to put the three powers in the same bucket in this area."
The expert believes Trump attended the meeting as he is "actively thinking about his legacy in the final two years in office."
"So, in this context, the idea of setting up a trilateral nuclear arms control arrangement would have been a very big achievement," Lee said.
But, in the end, the declaration said the countries would merely engage in "dialogue" on the issue, avoiding any explicit commitments to downsize their nuclear stockpiles.
A reluctant host?

China initially hesitated to organize the trilateral summit as it did not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm Beijing's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.
The Chinese government, which is working to rebalance economic ties with the EU, was also wary of appearing to form a G3 club with Washington and Moscow, which could alienate other global partners.
Chanlett-Avery said that China had some degree of discomfort in convening this meeting, worried about getting involved in Ukraine issues.

But Beijing eventually "managed to get the outcome they wanted" and kept the European conflict out of the meeting's focus, she noted. "China was able to show off Shenzhen and all of its sparkling high-tech features. They convened a successful international meeting that grabbed lots of headlines," she added. "So, I think China probably came out feeling okay."
Prior to the summit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of a "second Yalta," referring to the Yalta Conference held in Crimea in 1945.
That meeting saw the Allied powers decide on the post-war European order following the end of World War II.

In Shenzhen, Putin stressed that Russia, the US and China, as victors in World War II and veto-wielding members of the UN Security Council, bore a "joint responsibility for maintaining international peace."

But Ying-Yu Lin, Associate Professor at Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies at Taiwan's Tamkang University, said the Yalta comparison "is a bit of a stretch," given the vast differences between 1945 and now.
Why Russia and China aren't really best friends
Will there be more such trilaterals?
Putin also said that all three leaders "agree that it's a useful format," and such meetings could take place again.

Lee, the EIU expert, said the trilateral setup "is unlikely to be just a one-off" and there will likely be more such meetings in the coming years. "Especially from the US side to have this kind of setup, there will be some interest in maintaining warm relations with both China and Russia," he underlined.

articles.title: Anthropic stock soars over 20% in Nasdaq debut
articles.summary: Shares of Anthropic rose on their first day of trading, as investors weighted AI enthusiasm against a massive valuation and uncertain path to profitability.

image.caption: Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 US per share late Wednesday, above the $70 to $78 US range stated by the company in recent regulatory filings. (REUTERS/Dado Ruvic)

blocks.text: Business·Breaking
Shares of Anthropic rose on their first day of trading, as investors weighted AI enthusiasm against a massive valuation and uncertain path to profitability.
Anthropic's IPO is the largest on record
Shares of Anthropic have started trading on the Nasdaq, rising over 20 per cent on the AI giant’s first day as a public company.

The stock debuted slightly before noon Eastern Time on Thursday, at $111.50 US per share, according to Bloomberg. That’s 34 per cent above the $83 US initial public offering (IPO) announced by the AI giant behind the popular Claude chatbot late Wednesday.
Shares are up 20.85 per cent, as of 12:27 p.m. ET.

Considered the first-ever pure-play artificial intelligence stock, Thursday’s public market debut pits AI enthusiasm directly against concerns among investors about the company’s massive valuation, and uncertain path to profitability.

Anthropic shares are now well above the $70 to $78 US range the company stated in recent regulatory filings earlier this month. On Wednesday, it boosted the number of shares up for sale, pushing its valuation slightly above $1.5 trillion US.
The San Francisco-based company holds the record for the largest-ever IPO, raising $81 billion US, well ahead of SpaceX, which raised about $75 billion US in June.
Anthropic’s ticker symbol is “ANT.”

While Anthropic’s newly-minted stock is higher by double-digits today, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index is down slightly. AI-related stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology and CoreWeave are also slipping lower.
Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion US valuation is but a drop in a bucket compared with the size of the opportunity it’s spelling out for investors.

In regulatory filings, Anthropic points to more than $40 trillion US in annual economic value generated by knowledge workers globally as the broader opportunity for its technology. The filing also cites industry estimates projecting that AI solutions will create $22.5 trillion US in cumulative economic impact by 2031
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jeff Lagerquist is a senior writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Erin, Ont., he studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. Jeff previously worked as a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance Canada. He was also a reporter and digital producer for CTV National News, BNN Bloomberg and The Financial Post. In 2025, he was a Columbia University energy journalism fellow.

articles.title: Rohingya genocide: What was said in court and what happens now?
articles.summary: The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

blocks.text: Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.
The BBC's Anna Holligan is in the Hague and reports on what the ICJ's ruling means.

articles.title: Alberta bill would ban some bike lanes, let transportation minister remove others
articles.summary: Alberta’s government is proposing to ban future bike lanes that remove or restrict motor-vehicle traffic and give itself the power to remove some existing bike lanes.

image.caption: Bill 43 could allow bike lanes like this one, on Hermitage Road in northeast Edmonton, to be removed. (Scott Neufeld/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New
Alberta’s government is proposing to ban future bike lanes that remove or restrict motor-vehicle traffic and give itself the power to remove some existing bike lanes.
If passed, Bill 43 would raise fines for unsafe trucking operators, regulate personal e-scooters

Those changes are part of Bill 43, which the government is calling the Safe and Sensible Roads Act. It’s an omnibus bill that, in addition to bike lanes, seeks to increase penalties for unsafe commercial trucking operators, give the provincial government more oversight on municipal LRT projects and establish a framework and minimum safety standards for personal e-scooters and other similar devices.

According to a news release the government issued Thursday, the province will work with municipalities to ensure bike lanes are safely planned and fit within the broader transportation network. The proposed changes, the release said, would help make sure communities consider how bike lanes affect traffic flow, commuters, emergency services and the movement of goods.
Municipalities could request exemptions on a case-by-case basis, but must provide supporting information and rationale for the minister’s assessment, the release said.

items: Are people actually using Edmonton’s bike lanes? Here’s a look at the numbers

blocks.text: The proposed legislation does not include criteria municipalities must meet to qualify for exemptions, nor does it explain how bike lanes would be selected for removal and who would pay for removal costs.
If passed, the government expects the legislation would take effect in April, with regulations also scheduled to come in the spring.
Transportation Minister Devin Dreeshen has been saying for months that bike lanes make sense in some locations, but should not take away parking spaces or traffic lanes used by motor vehicles.

items: Alberta’s government asked residents to complain about bike lanes. Here’s what rolled in.

blocks.text: Some residents agree with the minister and have expressed their concerns about specific bike lanes with him. Bike lane supporters and urban planning experts have said bike lanes make roads safer for everyone and help reduce traffic.

Dreeshen told CBC News in August he was emboldened by the Ontario Court of Appeal, which overturned a lower court’s decision that the Ontario government’s plan to replace some bike lanes with car lanes was unconstitutional.

Alberta’s Safe and Sensible Roads Act, if passed by the Legislature, would also allow municipalities to authorize privately-owned and rented e-scooters — and other personal micromobility devices — and create rules for them that meet or exceed provincial minimum safety standards.
Currently, citizens in Calgary and Edmonton can ride e-scooters from companies like Lime, but Albertans can’t legally ride their own devices without exemptions from the province.

items: Alberta gov't mulling regulations around micromobility vehicles like e-scooters

blocks.text: The government also intends to change the name of the Public Transit and Green Infrastructure Project Act to the Urban Rail Transit Act.
This new act would apply to current and future urban rail transit lines and make municipalities tell the provincial cabinet minister about planned changes to them.
The government says these changes would expand provincial oversight and ensure cities’ LRT projects align with provincial priorities.

articles.title: US army plan to detonate bomb-making chemicals has Iowa residents bracing for lead dust cloud
articles.summary:
Officials recommend that residents in path of expected toxic plume vacate area, and some schools will be closed

Plans by the US army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals that…

blocks.text: Plans by the US army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals that have become unusable and might explode if moved have residents in south-east Iowa worried that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems.

The detonation at the Iowa army ammunition plant is scheduled for Friday, and officials recommend that some residents in nearby Middletown begin vacating the area that morning. If they cannot leave their homes, they should stay inside and keep windows and doors closed.

“The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” an advisory states. “Lead is toxic to humans and animals. The goal of this advisory is to provide the public with actionable information out of an abundance of caution to minimize lead exposure.”

Officials have released maps showing the potential for lead dust to drift north. Updated maps showed the plume’s shift, and the army will continue to update the map based on weather. Some schools in the path of the plume have already canceled classes.
Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but there are thousands more in the path of the plume.

The vibrations from the two blasts would not last long but could break old windows in town, and the resulting dust was expected to linger for no more than one hour, depending on wind speed, officials said.
While the army recommends cleaning cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces after the detonation, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough.
Surrounding communities get late notice

Middletown residents learned in March that the army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered.

“The safety of our people and our neighbors is non‑negotiable,” Lt Col Daniel Nosse, the commander of the plant, said at the time, acknowledging the volatility of the chemical compound used in munitions production.

The army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on 13 November approved an emergency permit, paving the way for Friday’s detonation.

That permit required the army to track specific rates of potential air and dust dispersion and notify the public five days in advance, prompting Sunday’s advisory to communities as far as 100 miles (160km) away.

Just a few miles north-west, the Danville community school district will close on Friday, the superintendent said in an announcement on Tuesday. Pat Wallace said his initial intention was to keep schools open, but there were enough uncertainties that made canceling “the most responsible decision”.
“I am not suggesting that the detonation will result in unsafe conditions,” he wrote. “The reality is that we simply do not know exactly what conditions will look like Friday afternoon.”

In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles (32km) north-east of the ammunition plant, city officials were approached about allowing soil, water and air testing late last month. But they only learned of their potential exposure on Sunday, when the initial map put them dead-center in the dust exposure area. Schools and the public library will close on Friday and the local fire department planned to hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles.
The city of nearly 2,000 residents was no longer in the plume in an updated map.

“This is probably a first for me. I believe it’s a first for a lot of our citizens,” the deputy city clerk, Amy Stucker, said on Wednesday. “The biggest issue we’re having is the lack of information.”
The office of the Iowa governor, Kim Reynolds, was first briefed on Monday about the public advisory, her office said.

News of the planned blasts also caught the attention of environmental and public health officials in Illinois. They urged the US military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state after the detonations.
Long-term storage leaves lead azide vulnerable

The barrels of lead azide had been stored at the ammunition plant for more than 20 years in earthen containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, public affairs specialist at the army sustainment command.

During a routine check earlier this year, the army found that some of the water had evaporated, causing the lead azide to crystallize. That makes it more sensitive to friction and shock, thus “creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation”, according to an emergency permit approved last week by the EPA.
Moving or relocating it posed an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation, officials said. Barati said that possibility increases in cold weather.
“We’re really concerned about the weather situation,” Barati said about moving forward with Friday’s detonation. “We’re really concerned that it will detonate on its own.”
The army said it put together a panel of experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with the detonation plan.
The barrels are surrounded above, below and on all sides with concrete, which is buried under soil. Sand barriers are stacked two storeys high around the soil.
During the detonation, the soil will be sprayed with water and the air will be misted to try to keep the majority of lead on army property, Barati said.
Young children are a particular concern for potential exposure

Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa’s department of occupational and environmental health, said it was encouraging to see that the army and the EPA were doing all they could to minimize the dust, but it was still unknown how much would end up in the atmosphere and on surfaces.

Lead is a neurological toxicant that can decrease brain activity and development, especially in young children, O’Shaughnessy said. He is particularly concerned for toddlers who are at the age of putting everything in their mouth.

According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the contents of the drums using other chemicals were considered. But officials said any plan that involved handling the drums would increase the probability of accidental, fatal detonation.

articles.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
articles.summary:
Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent

The

blocks.text: The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states.

In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent.
The lengthy judgment will have been read particularly carefully by Israel, the only other country currently before the ICJ accused of genocide.
It is also relevant to Germany, which has been brought before the court by Nicaragua on the accusation it has facilitated and failed to prevent genocide in Gaza.

“I think it’s a judgment that brings the genocide convention alive,” said Philippe Sands, a leading human rights lawyer who was part of the Gambian legal team. “It gives the convention practical, real meaning. And if the alternative view had been taken, the convention would essentially become a dead letter.”

Amnesty International’s secretary general, Agnès Callamard, called the ruling “a rare moment of justice for survivors, victims and their families”. But it was also an assertion of humanitarian law in an increasingly lawless world.

“This is a good day for international law. We needed it,” said Dr Iva Vukušić, an assistant professor in international History at Utrecht University and a war crimes expert. “It is really important, clarifying a lot of law, and that’s going to be very helpful going forward.”

There will be a spillover from this ruling to its sister tribunal in The Hague, the international criminal court (ICC), providing a benchmark for when genocide charges could be made against individual perpetrators.

The Trump administration, instinctively hostile to international legal institutions, is also watching critically. The US ambassador to the UN told the ICJ before this judgment not to “lower the legal threshold for proving genocide” lest it be “weaponised” against US and allied soldiers.
The court did not directly lower the standard for demonstrating genocide, and the Gambia – which brought the case to The Hague – did not ask it to.

The judges kept the existing benchmark for judging genocide intent as the “only reasonable inference” of Myanmar’s actions and referred extensively to prior case law. But it went a long way towards clarifying how that standard should be applied in assessing atrocity crimes committed by states.

Before this case, only Serbia had faced the charge of genocide at the ICJ, in cases brought by Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Bosnian ruling in 2007, Belgrade was found to have failed to prevent the 1995 genocide in Srebrenica, but in both cases it was cleared of committing the genocide directly.

The new ICJ judgment finds the Myanmar military directly responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, a Muslim minority targeted in a ferocious counterinsurgency campaign that reached its peak in 2017.

In assessing the Myanmar campaign, the ICJ looked not just at the death toll of about 10,000 in assessing the scale of the atrocities, but at the total Rohingya population targeted in northern Rakhine state, 815,000 people. Significantly, it cast its net wider than just the death toll, considering mental damage done to the survivors, particularly victims of sexual violence, and the impact on reproduction in the Rohingya community.

Most importantly, the ICJ judgment provided a guide to interpreting the standard set by Serbian cases, in which a finding of genocide could be made only if there were not other plausible motives for mass killing.

In this judgment, the court ruled that Myanmar could have had other motives, such as the desire to displace or punish the Rohingya population, but that those motives could exist alongside genocidal intent. The judges said genocidal intent was the “only reasonable inference” from the “totality” of evidence.

In justifying that conclusion the judges pointed to several factors that international law experts say are relevant to the Gaza case, which is now hearing written pleadings and is expected to take at least another three years.

The common factors include the targeting of children, which the court described as striking at the “foundation” of the Rohingya as a group – the ICJ said up to 2,109 Rohingya children under the age of five had been killed, while more than 5,000 Palestinian children under five years old have been killed in the Gaza war.

Another incriminating factor cited by the court was the “bulldozing and large-scale terrain clearance” after the destruction of villages, followed by “rapid construction” including security installations, which has been the hallmark of Israeli army occupation of over 60% of the Gaza Strip.

“It’s full of messages for Israel,” said William Schabas, an international law professor and expert on genocide at Middlesex University. “There are obvious differences, of course, the evidence will be different, but if you exchanged the word Myanmar with Israel, you wouldn’t have to change much in the judgment.”

The fact that there were six dissenting voices on the bench suggested that substantial parts of the majority’s reasoning were not beyond dispute, and lawyers involved in the case cautioned that it did not necessarily mean that the same bench would find Israel guilty of genocide in Gaza. But the same lawyers added that the opposite was almost certainly true. If this case had failed, the case brought by South Africa against Israel would have been all but over.

articles.title: US zoo staff monitor Fiona the hippo’s rear end for signs of hat she ate
articles.summary:
Colonoscopy, ultrasound, Vibration plate and patience deployed 11 days after beloved beast ingested knitted hat

Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has undergone a…

blocks.text: Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has undergone a colonoscopy amid efforts to remove a knitted hat which she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure.
With surgery too risky for a full-grown hippos like Fiona, who weighs in the region of 2,500 pounds (1,113kg), veterinarians tried an alternative method of getting the hat to pass through her system.

The hat fell near Fiona when a visitor to Cincinnati Zoo tossed it in the air bouncing it off a ceiling fan and causing it to fall into the enclosure, according to the Associated Press. Fiona ate the hat and was initially asymptomatic.
Days later, however, she began to lose appetite and staff at the zoo were forced to feed Fiona more in the hope that she would eventually get the hat through her digestive system.
The zoo announced on Wednesday that the animal care team was using a vibration plate from a horse farm to help move things along, according to the Associated Press.

Fiona was sedated a second time on Tuesday for evaluation. After an ultrasound, veterinarians could see her intestines still trying push the hat through. They also used a 9ft scope colonoscopy to view her intestines as well.

“The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the zoo said on social media. Fiona will remain out of her enclosure while she is receiving treatment.
Footage from the procedure released by the Zoo on Wednesday shows her snorting and moving around her enclosure, which vets says is a sign of progress. Her hydration levels are still being monitored.

“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked, and they were happy to see her respond. Thank you for your continued love and concern for Fiona and her dedicated care team,” the zoo said.

This is not the first time Fiona’s health has been at risk. She became a global sensation after her premature birth in 2017 when she couldn’t stand on her own and weighed just 29lb at birth, 25lb less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

Fiona’s recovery has garnered support from across the country including, apparently, from Timothy, another hippo at the San Antonio zoo. Timothy sent well wishes via Instagram. “I know you’ve got some amazing people looking after you. We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!”
Zoo staff said updates on Fiona’s rally back to health will come as they get more information, reminding visitors to be careful when near habitats and to secure belongings.
In the meantime, the zoo asks visitors, “If something falls into a habitat, please notify a zoo staff member immediately.”

articles.title: Duterte's defense witness admits Cale88 has 'red flags'
articles.summary: A defense witness in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte admitted that there were "red flags" in the operations of Cale88 but said these do not necessarily mean wrongdoing.

blocks.text: Published November 20, 2026 1:12am

A witness for the defense in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte admitted that there were "red flags" in the operations of Cale88, but maintained that these do not necessarily mean wrongdoing.

Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros asked AML Consulting PH head Rainer Dela Fuente whether he knew if Cale88—the food company being linked to Duterte's spouse Manases Carpio—had a legitimate explanation for its suspicious transactions reports to the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC).
Dela Fuente replied in the negative.
“Masasabi niyo po bang unusual itong total of 757 CTRs and STRs na may halagang P1,245,736,297.8?” Hontiveros asked.
(Would you say that having 757 covered transaction reports [CTRs] and suspicious transaction reports [STRs] worth P1,245,736,297.8 is unusual?)
Dela Fuente said that only the AMLC could determine if this was suspicious, but maintained that suspicion is not a direct indication of unlawful activity.
He said that there are with many more CTRs and STRs than what Cale88 had.
Hontiveros asked about the AMLC's flagging Cale88’s two employees, as well as its transactions with China.
"Lastly po, Attorney De La Fuente, hindi po ba yan posibleng mga [are these not possible] red flags?" Hontiveros asked.
"Yes, these are red flags po that merit…scrutiny, review, opo, but again red flags po are not direct evidence of wrongdoing, " Dela Fuente replied.

During Hontiveros’ questioning, Dela Fuente also said that he previously worked with gambling businesses and Philippine Offshore Gaming Operators. He was also a previous consultant for the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR). — BM, GMA News
