articles.title: Look up and give Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk a wave! The International Space Station is flying overhead
articles.summary: For the next few weeks — if you have clear skies — you can watch the International Space Station fly overhead in the evenings. If you see it, you could maybe give a little wave to Canadian Space…

image.caption: The International Space Station is pictured from the SpaceX Crew Dragon Endeavour during a fly around of the orbiting lab on Nov. 8, 2021. (NASA)

blocks.text: Science

For the next few weeks — if you have clear skies — you can watch the International Space Station fly overhead in the evenings. If you see it, you could maybe give a little wave to Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk as he whizzes by at 7.66 kilometres a second.
ISS will be visible on clear evenings over the next few weeks
For the next few weeks — if you have clear skies — you can watch the International Space Station (ISS) fly overhead in the evenings.
If you see it, you could maybe give a little wave to Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk as he whizzes by at 7.66 kilometres a second.
Kutryk is just one of seven crew members working and living on board the orbiting laboratory as part of Expedition 75.
Since arriving on the ISS on Oct. 1, Kutryk has been hard at work with various experiments and tasks, including a recent one on cardiac research.

items: Crew-13 astronauts, including Canada's Joshua Kutryk, board the ISS after trip from Earth

blocks.text: And to no one's surprise, he's also been enjoying the view.
The ISS is often visible over Canada as it orbits the Earth. But over the coming weeks it will be visible in the evening sky, rather than the early-morning passes it's been making recently.
How to find the ISS in the sky

Very simply, it will look like a very bright white dot — compared to the thousands of fainter lights you might see that are satellites — moving across the sky. It won't have any blinking lights like airplanes and it will move steadily in one direction.

items: Joshua Kutryk says he's 'having a blast' on the International Space Station
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk conducts his 1st spacewalk

blocks.text: Now you have to find out when the ISS will be passing overhead. There are a few ways you can do this.

One is heavens-above.com, an independent website that tracks various satellites and spacecraft. There, you can sign up with your location and find the ISS in a list of other visible objects. It will then provide you with a chart of times like the one below.
This chart shows the times the ISS will be visible over Toronto over the next couple of weeks. (Heavens-above.com)
When it comes to the brightness, the more negative a number, the brighter it will appear (it doesn't appear to make sense, but that's astronomy for you).
Click on the date, and it will show you a map of the night sky with a line crossing various constellations, representing the path of the ISS.
This map of the night sky shows the constellations and the path the ISS will take on this particular pass. (Heavens-above.com)
If you only see a short line near the horizon on the map, you can probably skip that date, as the ISS may be trickier to see.
If it’s a longer line, you can give it a try, so long as you have an unobstructed view.
The constellation map will also show you the local times when the ISS will be in the sky, which is incredibly helpful.

items: A spacewalk to remember: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says seeing Earth 'changed' him

blocks.text: NASA’s Spot the Station app is another great resource.

When you open the app, it should automatically detect your location. On the home screen it will provide you with a countdown to the ISS pass. The "Sightings" button will provide you with a list of upcoming passes.
It also has a feature called AR View (augmented reality), which gives you details of the sky when you hold your phone up to it — including a line showing you where the ISS will pass.
If you can find the ISS and watch it cross the sky, just think: maybe Joshua Kutryk is looking back at you.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science. You can send her story ideas at nicole.mortillaro@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Juliet Daniel changed cancer research. Students of the late Canadian scientist say she also changed lives
articles.summary: Friends, students and colleagues gathered this week at McMaster University in Hamilton to celebrate Juliet Daniel, a Barbadian-Canadian professor and scientist who died April 28 at age 61. They…

image.caption: Juliet Daniel, a Barbadian-Canadian professor, scientist and community advocate, was 61 when she passed away on April 28. (Submitted by Juliet Daniel)

blocks.text: Shaiya Robinson saw something she hadn't seen before — a Black woman leading a cancer research lab — when she was a student and first met Juliet Daniel at McMaster University for an interview in 2009.
Robinson, who had rarely encountered Black professors, said the meeting to join the lab was about more than an interview. It was the first time she could picture herself in that position.
"I'd never had a Black professor before."
Daniel became her supervisor, mentor and, eventually, a colleague.
Now, Robinson is an assistant professor at McMaster, carrying forward many of the lessons she learned from the woman who helped make that future possible.

Robinson was among former students, friends and colleagues who gathered Monday at McMaster University to honour the legacy of Daniel. The Barbadian-Canadian professor and scientist was a longtime breast cancer survivor who died on April 28 at age 61.
"She was such a pivotal person in every step of my career journey and my personal journey," Robinson recalled.
Determined to ask different questions
Daniel joined McMaster in November 1999 as an assistant professor, becoming the first Black woman faculty member in the university's faculty of science.
Her research focused on understanding why certain cancers impact some populations more than others, and why outcomes can differ.
She was internationally recognized for her research into triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), an aggressive form of the disease that disproportionately affects Black and Hispanic women.

Her work helped advance understanding of the genetic differences behind cancer outcomes, including her discovery of a gene she named Kaiso, after a style of calypso music rooted in her Caribbean heritage.
Michele James knew Daniel for about 30 years and sits on the board of The Olive Branch of Hope (TOBOH), a breast cancer support organization.
James said Daniel was looking into health equity and reducing health-care disparities long before it became a mainstream conversation.
"She was a real trailblazer in that regard."

Daniel co-founded organizations including the African Caribbean Faculty Association of McMaster, the Canadian Black Scientists Network, the McMaster Academic Women’s Success and Mentorship Lecture Series, and the Canadian Multicultural LEAD Organization for Mentoring and Training. (Paul Smith/CBC)
Made time for students, community
Robinson said Daniel had a demanding schedule, but somehow always made students and colleagues feel they had her full attention.
"She didn't have time, but she always made you feel like there was time for you."
Daniel also mentored Kevin Kelly, who now works in biotechnology.

Kelly met Daniel in 2000, when he was an undergraduate student looking for a supervisor for his research project. He stayed in her lab through his PhD, becoming the first doctoral graduate from her research group.
Kelly said Daniel was someone who took mentorship seriously and was generous with her time.
"She was always thinking about her students."
He said he admired her willingness to pursue questions that drew little scientific attention, particularly around cancer in Black women.
Kevin Kelly and Dr. Shaiya Robinson, left to right, were both mentored by Daniel. They remember her for her scientific accomplishments and compassionate style of mentoring. (Jeffery Tram/CBC)

Daniel also helped build a stronger community for Black academics. She co-founded the African Caribbean Faculty Association of McMaster and the Canadian Black Scientists Network, along with several other initiatives supporting mentorship, inclusion and student success.

"I was really proud of her for taking that very courageous step," James said. "She was already busy and that was something else that she took on to help advance things not for herself, but for the other faculty members."
Proud to be Bajan
For Stephanie Roberts, Daniel was first and foremost a childhood friend.

The two grew up in the same neighbourhood in Barbados, meeting when Roberts was about three and Daniel was five. They remained close even after Daniel moved to Canada and Roberts immigrated to the United States.
Roberts recalled Daniel's determination to make a difference in cancer research, particularly after her mother died of the disease.
She said Daniel initially pursued medicine before choosing research as a way to help find better answers for people affected by cancer.
"It was never about the money," Roberts said. "She truly wanted a cure for cancer."

items: To confront race in Canada, she became a beauty queen, a tour guide and a time traveller

blocks.text: Although they were in different job fields, Daniel would sometimes invite Roberts to tag along on work trips.
She also remembers Daniel as a longtime friend from her home country.
Daniel loved calypso music, dancing, cooking and hosting friends, and was an accomplished ballroom dancer who won several awards, Roberts said.
She said Daniel never made a point of introducing herself by her title, despite her academic achievements.
"If you went anywhere with her, she always went and said, 'Hi, I'm Juliet.'"
Pioneering cancer researcher wants more diversity in STEM fields
Roberts says Daniel was always proud to be from Barbados and would do whatever she could to give back.
James said Daniel helped the island during the COVID-19 pandemic by connecting its government with people who could facilitate access to vaccines, medical expertise and supplies.

Daniel's contributions earned her numerous honours, including being named a Distinguished University Professor in 2025, McMaster's highest recognition for faculty members. Her research has been cited more than 6,400 times.
In 2024, the federal government's Canadian Intellectual Property Office named Daniel as one of three Black Innovators in Research and Medicine.
Roberts hopes Daniel's name will be permanently recognized, including at a potential tribute at McMaster and possibly seeing Barbados's living lab named after her.
"It's just sad that in most cases, we have to wait on some till someone passes to celebrate them."
Robinson said she wants to continue Daniel's example by making mentorship a priority for her own students.
The event to honour Daniel drew friends, colleagues, students and mentees to the McLean Centre for Collaborative Discovery at McMaster University. (Jeffery Tram/CBC)
During Monday's celebration, James shared a quote that she said captured Daniel's approach to life: "It's better to light one small candle than to curse the darkness."
James noted that the celebration drew many people whose lives were touched by Daniel.
"She was like a candle that you can just take that candle and use it to light lots and lots of other candles," she said.
"And as I looked out into the room this afternoon, I felt that there were so many candles that had been lit initially by Juliet, and that their light would carry on indefinitely."

For more stories about the experiences of Black Canadians — from anti-Black racism to success stories within the Black community — check out Being Black in Canada, a CBC project Black Canadians can be proud of. You can read more stories here.
(CBC)

articles.title: Locker room at Montreal’s Olympic sports complex 'falling apart' just months after reno
articles.summary: Less than a year after a multimillion-dollar revitalization of the aging locker room at Montreal’s Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard, athletes say they've had to navigate cold or broken showers,…

image.caption: Since the Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard locker rooms reopened to the public in March, users report issues with plumbing such as toilet water running hot, showers running cold as well as leaks from the ceilings. (Douglas Gelevan/ CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal

Less than a year after a multimillion-dollar revitalization of the aging locker room at Montreal’s Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard, athletes say they've had to navigate cold or broken showers, water fountains with undrinkable hot water and crumbling tiling.
City acknowledges issues with $61.4M interior renovation phase of Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard
Hot water in the drinking fountains. Showers running cold. Crumbling tiles. Water leaking from the ceiling.
Less than a year after a multimillion-dollar revitalization of the aging locker room at Montreal’s Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard, athletes are unimpressed with the results.
“I couldn’t believe that so quickly, so fast it was all coming apart,” said Mara Do Santos, who swims in a masters club at Claude-Robillard three days a week.
Émilie Masson, another swimmer with the same group, was most perplexed by hot water in the toilets.
“It's like, 'Wow. Who didn’t do his job?'”
Many of the new showers were taped off and out of order when CBC visited the locker room on Nov. 6. (Douglas Gelevan/CBC)

The locker room at the facility built for the 1976 Olympics closed in August 2024, when the city launched its latest interior phase of an overall $166-million project to modernize the entire complex. It reopened in March 2026.
During CBC’s visit on Nov. 6, at least seven showers were closed and marked “out of order.”
There was also evidence of several leaks in the new ceiling.
In addition to the significant plumbing issues, CBC also noted cosmetic problems such as tiles coming off of walls, hooks missing from their anchors in the changing rooms and rust around the drains.
“It’s brand new — literally,” Do Santos says.
Parts of Montreal's Claude-Robillard sports complex falling apart after $61M refresh
Olympic legacy
The Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard was originally built for the 1976 Olympic Games when it hosted events such as handball and waterpolo.
It continues to be an important training facility for many Olympic hopefuls in sports like swimming, diving, and track and field.
“This is a top notch sports facility that we have to keep,” Do Santos says.
CBC found several spots in the new ceiling that showed evidence of water damage. (Douglas Gelevan/CBC)
The renovation project to modernize Claude-Robillard was first announced in 2016.
A $61.4-million interior renovations phase that included the locker room and pool mechanical systems began in 2024. Work on the overall project is expected to continue in stages through 2029.
But Masson says that if the quality of work on the locker room is any indication of what's to come, taxpayers should be worried.
Only months after reopening, some tiles are already falling off the walls inside the locker room at the Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard (Douglas Gelevan/CBC)
“The big renovation itself is not done. The locker room, apparently, it's done. But it’s falling apart,” Masson says. “Can’t we have a good quality that will last?”
The City of Montreal did not respond to CBC’s request for an interview.

But in an email, city spokesperson Kim Nantais Desormiers acknowledged there are issues and went on to say that the city is following up with contractors and subcontractors that worked on the locker room.
A shower grate is showing signs of rust only months after the newly renovated locker room in Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard reopened to the public. (Douglas Gelevan/CBC)
Problems with pool renovations
Swimmers told CBC the issues with the interior renovations extend to the Olympic-sized pool where they train.
Like the locker room, it was also closed in August 2024. Do Santos says the problems began as soon as it reopened in November 2025.
She said the new movable bulkhead, a kind of floating bridge, would not stay in place.
At one point, her swim team was forced to improvise and use their own ratchet straps to fix it into position, she said.

Émilie Masson, left, and Mara Do Santos, right, use the pool and locker room at Claude-Robillard three times a week and are frustrated to see so many issues come up with the newly renovated spaces. (Charles Contant/CBC)
There are also ongoing issues with the filtration system. The swimmers say the water in the pool is cloudy. The city says it's working to resolve that problem.

In another email to CBC, Nantais Desormiers added that the general contractor responsible for the pool and the locker room will “handle any repairs covered by the applicable warranties” and that all other work will be carried out by the city's municipal maintenance crews.
At this point, no additional costs are anticipated, she says.
Investigation finds breach of municipal regulations
This isn’t the first time the renovations at the sports complex have caused friction.
The office of Montreal's inspector general looked into how the contract for the swimming pool was awarded after receiving a tip from a whistleblower in August 2024.

In a June 2026 report, the office found breaches of municipal regulations by the engineering consulting firm GBI Experts-Conseils Inc. It also highlighted oversight shortcomings within the city's property management department (SGPI).

GBI was awarded an $11.5-million professional services contract in 2022. The investigation concluded that GBI violated regulations by appointing a project manager who was not qualified and that the subsequent call to tenders was compromised and not a fair process.

Mireille Beaudin, director of strategic consulting services for GBI, said in a statement to CBC the company strongly disputes the report’s findings and that it is committed to the “highest ethical and professional standards.”
Work continues at Complexe Sportif Claude-Robillard. A $61.4-million phase of interior renovations began in 2024 that included the locker room and pool mechanical systems. (Douglas Gelevan/CBC)
The inspector general recommended the city impose a $100,000 fine on GBI — the maximum authorized — and that the SGPI reform its vetting processes.
The inspector general says the city has yet to move forward on its recommendations or fine GBI.
City spokesperson Nantais Desormiers says the issue is before the executive council.

articles.title: VIA Rail heading back to Quebec’s Gaspé region after 15 years — a partial win that brings hope
articles.summary: Gaspé residents who have been waiting for the return of passenger train service since 2011 hope new federal investments and commitments from VIA Rail will lead to full service resumption down the…

image.caption: Eileen Jessop said that as a young adult, she could walk to her local train station in Chandler, Que., and get off in downtown Montreal the next morning. (Julia Page/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal·New

Gaspé residents who have been waiting for the return of passenger train service since 2011 hope new federal investments and commitments from VIA Rail will lead to full service resumption down the line.
VIA Rail route to New Carlisle, Que., expected to resume by spring 2028
After 15 years of lobbying for the return of passenger train service to the Gaspé region, residents are finally seeing light at the end of the tunnel.

VIA Rail confirms it will resume partial service along the Baie des Chaleurs, reaching New Carlisle, Que., by spring 2028. This commitment from the Crown corporation paired with a $1.2 billion investment over three years for VIA Rail are fuelling hope full service to the Gaspé region — including the city that bears the same name — could return after a 15-year absence.
But the Quebec government needs to jump on board.

"It's great news in itself," said Éric Dubé, mayor of New Richmond and president of Société du chemin de fer de la Gaspésie (SCFG), a local non-profit organization in charge of repairing and operating the tracks.
The last passenger train reached the city of Gaspé in December 2011, after the tracks were deemed unsafe. In 2013, the final stop became Matapédia, leaving a 325-kilometre stretch without service.
For residents, news of the partial return of passenger train service brings back memories of an era when travelling to and from the Gaspé region was much more accessible.
"Back in the good years of the 1990s, as many as 28,000 passengers a year would take the train to the Gaspé Peninsula — so we’d love to be able to see that happen again someday," said Dubé.
The return of passenger train service to New Carlisle will cut the driving distance in half for travellers headed to Gaspé. (Lorena Suárez del Real/CBC)
The province, which has owned the tracks since 2015, has invested $350 million so far, which enabled the partial return of freight trains to the region.
Until now, VIA Rail was steadfast in its position to only bring back service to the region if the full line was refurbished, said Dubé.
"Before it was [all the way to the city of] Gaspé or nothing. Now they are agreeing to a partial return to New Carlisle, but with the objective the tracks be refurbished all the way to Gaspé."
The final stop for shipping goods is currently near the cement plant in Port-Daniel-Gascons.
VIA Rail’s partial return to Quebec’s Gaspé region — after 15 years — sparks hope

VIA Rail confirmed to CBC by e-mail the service between Quebec City and New Carlisle would run two to three times a week in a "phased return of service," while "working with the government of Quebec, infrastructure owners, local communities and all partners involved to move this important project forward."
Rail crucial for access to health care, local businesses

Dubé hopes the next provincial budget will include money to repair the last section of tracks between Port-Daniel-Gascons and Gaspé. That is also an ongoing demand from the local citizens' committee that has been at the forefront of the battle to bring back the train.
Residents on the Gaspé peninsula have been campaigning for the return of passenger train service since VIA Rail cut back service in 2011. (Julia Page/CBC)
"It's really disappointing to see how much the service has degraded in my lifetime," said Eileen Jessop, with the Coalition pour le retour des services d'un train de passagers en Gaspésie.

Jessop said going to see a show or visit family in Montreal used to be as simple as walking to the station in Chandler to board a night train. Now travelling back and forth to Matapedia adds on hours of driving.
"It's rough on the roads, it's rough on our vehicles, it's rough on our mental health."

items: Canada's 'Railway City' wants passenger trains back. Like in much of the country, it's not so simple

blocks.text: Many people who live in the region, including seniors, don't have access to a car, said Jessop, and often need to travel to Quebec City or Montreal to see medical specialists. The coalition also wants the province and VIA rail to arrange for more comfortable wagons designed for health care transportation.
Quebec’s new Transport Minister Nicolas Girard said there were no new developments for the moment, but his office said "an update could be made further down the line."

After numerous announcements from the province over the years to finalize repairs on the tracks, the project was sent back to the 'planning stage' in Quebec's 2025 infrastructure plan. (Julia Page/CBC)
Meanwhile, the Ministry of Transport "continues to work with VIA Rail with the aim of a resumption of passenger service," Girard's office said in a statement.
For Jessop, if rail service comes back, she wants to tick travelling from Gaspé to Vancouver off her bucket list.
"If the train comes back that's going to be one of my first things — taking the Canadian to the other side."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Julia Page is a radio and online journalist with CBC News, based in Quebec City. Her role is to travel to communities across the province, from Gaspé to Trois-Rivières to Rouyn-Noranda, to meet with Quebecers and reflect the issues affecting their communities. She can be reached at julia.page@cbc.ca.

blocks.text: 'God, protect us from such friends,' Poland's Tusk says after Trump's 'he's my friend' comments to Putin
Poland’s prime minister Donald Tusk – one of Europe’s five negotiators – does not seem to be impressed by what he saw in Shenzhen.
“God, protect us from such friends,” he said on X in an apparent reference to Trump’s enthusiastic greeting with Putin.
Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski was similarly alarmed, telling reporters:

“Indeed, it is difficult to judge, by their fruits we shall know them, but the optics of this hugging Putin, calling him a friend, causes us some concern. Because the question arises – who is he more of a friend with, Putin or our president? And what will he possibly do if push comes to shove, which friend will he choose?”

On Ukraine, Trump says at the beginning of the trilateral meeting:

“We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. God knows what that’s supposed to mean in practice.

articles.title: Violent protests and killings in Bangladesh ahead of exiled Sheikh Hasina’s planned return
articles.summary:
Awami League party called for ⁠nationwide protest on Thursday after the government rejected Hasina’s request for passport

Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by…

blocks.text: Parts of Bangladesh were shut down Thursday as protests by supporters of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina sparked clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks, with the ancestral home ⁠of former leader Muhammad Yunus set ablaze in the violence.

Hasina’s Awami League party had called for a ​week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support ‌for Hasina’s planned return in December, culminating in a ‌nationwide lockdown on Thursday.

Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent ⁠protests demanding her resignation in August 2024, has requested a new passport and identity card to facilitate her return. Her supporters are protesting against the government’s rejection of that request.
To deter ⁠violence, 97 platoons of the Bangladesh Border Guard fanned out across seven districts, including Gopalganj and Faridpur, considered to have many Hasina supporters, a spokesperson ⁠said.
Police said former interim leader Yunus’ ancestral home in Chattogram, about 300km (186 miles) south-east of Dhaka, ​was set on fire late on ‌Wednesday.
It is likely that flammable ‌substances were thrown into an unused ground-floor room, police told Reuters, adding that Yunus’ paternal family members, who live on the upper floors, are safe.

blocks.caption: Fire engulfs the Tungipara police station in Gopalganj on 17 November amid unrest after the arrest of activists of the banned Awami League party.  Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Reuters could not immediately reach the Yunus Centre thinktank that speaks on his behalf to seek comment. Yunus and his government, which led Bangladesh after Hasina’s ouster, have faced hostility from her supporters.

During the last 10 days of protests, police have reported dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of ‌vehicles being set afire in at least 28 districts, injuring several police officials and members of the public, media have said.
Late on Tuesday, an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest near Hasina’s home district of Gopalganj, police said.

On the same night, a crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of cultural affairs minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and shops ‌belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.
On Wednesday morning, a bus company helper was burnt to death in the southern district of Pirojpur after two buses ​were set on fire, authorities said.

Tuesday marks a year since Hasina was ​sentenced to death by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on a student-led uprising against her in 2024. She has lived in exile in neighbouring India since fleeing Dhaka.
On Thursday, authorities detained former education minister Nurul Islam Nahid, who faces charges ⁠over several killings during the 2024 protests, from his house in Dhaka, police told Reuters.

At ​least 37 branches and offices of ​Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, have been targeted in arson attacks or ​attempted fires since 10 November, ‌with 14 more ​attacked since midnight ​on Tuesday, the bank said.

On Tuesday, the home minister Salahuddin Ahmed accused Awami League leaders abroad of inciting supporters to destabilise Bangladesh and torch property, adding that those involved in violence would be identified and prosecuted.
Awami League leaders, most of them in hiding, could not be reached for comment.

articles.title: Tammy Shipley was supposed to be monitored in prison. Instead she died after drinking 20L of water
articles.summary:
If the Aboriginal woman had been checked at regular intervals as required, her ‘excess consumption of water’ would have been prevented, inquest finds

• Warning: This article contains…

blocks.text: The death of an Aboriginal woman who collapsed after drinking at least 20 litres of water in a New South Wales prison cell was preventable and the result of systemic failures, a coroner has found.
Tammy Michelle Shipley, 47, died at Silverwater women’s correctional centre on 20 December 2022.
State coroner Teresa O’Sullivan ruled on Thursday that her death was caused by low blood sodium levels resulting from excessive water consumption and complications of schizoaffective disorder.
“I’m confident in finding that Tammy’s death was preventable,” O’Sullivan said.

The mother-of-five had been taken into custody on remand 11 days earlier, after being charged with shoplifting offences, but didn’t disclose her mental health issues to police. Police also didn’t double-check her answers about her health, despite the fact she had attended a police station two weeks earlier and told them she heard her neighbour talking in her head.
O’Sullivan found there had been a missed opportunity to recognise the mental health issues that were present, and to potentially divert Shipley away from the criminal justice system.

When she appeared in a local court over the shoplifting charges the next day, the magistrate was not told she had been refused bail on other charges, so made orders they thought would secure her release.
“There was a clear systems failure,” O’Sullivan found.
Shipley should have been continually monitored – both physically and electronically – after twice attempting self-harm in custody.
It was a serious failure that this had not been done, O’Sullivan said.
“If observations had been carried out at the intervals required, it was likely that Tammy’s excess consumption of water would have been … prevented,” she said.
She deemed it unsatisfactory that Shipley had not been seen by a psychiatrist or mental health nurse at any point during the 11 days before her death.

She added that Shipley should have received medical care from the time she started vomiting, after 10am on the day of her death. Instead, she said, Shipley experienced seizures shortly before noon and was seen lying face down on the floor of her cell around an hour later.
A period of 23 minutes lapsed between when she was first seen lying on the ground and the commencement of resuscitation attempts, which the coroner found was unacceptable.
One corrective services officer had hastily closed the door to her cell after smelling faeces in the room earlier in the day.
“It was completely inappropriate that Tammy, who was known to be suffering a mental health condition, was left in that condition in her cell,” O’Sullivan said.

O’Sullivan made 10 recommendations to NSW police, Corrective Services NSW and Justice Health, including a review of the “austere and depressing” unit in which Shipley was held, which was intended to be a therapeutic space but left the coroner gravely concerned.
after newsletter promotion
She also recommended regular monitoring of footage inside the jail and improved maintenance and cross-checking of records related to mental health conditions.
The coroner acknowledged the jail had already made changes after Shipley’s death.
Outside the court, Shipley’s mother, Vicki, said she hoped the findings would force the system to assess how people are treated.
“I honestly thought that at this stage of our country’s development, we have moved past how convicts were treated,” she said.
“The system – every system – eventually caused trauma to my daughter, until eventually it killed her.”
Vickey Shipley urged the NSW government to quickly implement the recommendations.
“If they’re not made, there will be some other family standing here doing exactly the same thing that I am,” she said.
“All too often we hear the cry: ‘There’s not enough money.’
“How much is a life worth?”

articles.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
articles.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still…

image.caption: Anthropic is aiming for a valuation of more than $1 trillion when it goes public next weekImage: Carlos Barria/REUTERS

blocks.text: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, is made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record.
The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50.
The opening price values the five-year-old firm at around $2 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.
Anthropic's public listing is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.
2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar bet on what US President Donald Trump calls superintelligence (SI) started paying off.
In the first half of the year, it did. Many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.
Post-midterm AI sell-off rattles global markets amid Big Tech jitters
AI doubts trigger market turbulence
The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty.
While the stock of chipmaker Nvidia pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen erratic movements in their stock prices.
Then, after the Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, technology stocks sold off again dramatically.
The Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — lost more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.
In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit last week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days.
The sell-off followed revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang resigned from the chipmaker, sending Nvidia's shares lower still and prompting a campaign by current and former staffers, investors and other key figures in Silicon Valley to have him reinstated.

blocks.caption: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is under scrutiny over an affair with an alleged Chinese spyImage: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO

While OpenAI — the maker of ChatGPT — has delayed its public listing until next year, some analysts have been left scratching their heads at Anthropic's decision to proceed, even though the IPO is reportedly about six times oversubscribed.
"Is this the best timing?" asked Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, in an interview with DW last week.
Dick said Anthropic's valuation depends on whether it can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."
Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude maker's prospects.

"Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg last week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize."
Fears that Democrats could regulate AI lead to global market bloodbath
Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive
Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending.
In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dick quipped, borrowing a line from the classic movie "The Wizard of Oz," which means times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money."
AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction'

Other analysts, however, think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks the post-election rout was a "healthy correction."
"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.
Signs to watch, not reasons to flee

With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported recently.
"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."
That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.
Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers, due to pressure on local water and electricity supplies.
Why US voters are fighting Trump's AI data center boom
Is AI next in a long line of bubbles that burst?

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railways, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.
Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.
"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.
Editor's note: This article was first published on November 13, 2026 and was updated on November 18 and 19 to reflect the latest developments.

articles.title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
articles.summary:
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four…

blocks.text: The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.

Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.
“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.

Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.

blocks.caption: A datacentre under construction at the Google Storey County campus in Sparks, Nevada, US. Photograph: Daniel Cole/Reuters

blocks.text: Datacentre developers have emerged as the world’s biggest corporate buyers of renewable energy to help fuel their servers which have a connection to local power grids. Despite this, the report showed that the appetite for fossil fuels is expected to grow even faster, particularly in the US and China.

By the end of the decade, around half of the electricity needed to power China’s AI datacentres will come from coal power plants, according to the IEA. The rest will come from renewable energy, with smaller amounts from nuclear reactors and very little from gas plants.

In contrast, the US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. There were plans for about 180GW of new gas-fired power plants linked to US datacentres in August this year, the agency said. That is almost as much new gas capacity as the total now installed across the European Union.
As a result of the growth in fossil fuel generation for datacentres, emissions associated with this sector were on track to rise by 70% by 2030, the IEA said.

The appetite for gas power among US datacentre developers is more than 16 times higher than in Canada, where the IEA identified plans for 11GW of gas generation to power their servers. In the rest of the world, AI developers have put forward plans for new gas plants with a combined capacity of just 4GW, the agency said.

This is because renewable energy is expected to play a greater role in supplying datacentres outside the US and China. In the EU, the IEA expects datacentres to rely on renewables for about 70% of their electricity by 2030 – followed by nuclear power, gas generation, and a very small amount of coal power.

blocks.caption: Workers at TikTok’s datacentre in Hamar, Norway. Photograph: Victoria Klesty/Reuters

blocks.text: The agency based its forecasts for the notoriously opaque industry on data showing the annual global shipment of AI servers, which have climbed eighteen-fold since 2020. It also used space-based imagery to track the buildout of 93 large “AI factories” around the world.

Its analysis suggests that the world’s datacentre capacity has climbed tenfold in the last 24 months to 17GW. By the time the AI factories were completed, their combined capacity was likely to be about 50GW, the IEA said.

The world’s existing stock of datacentres, including those with AI-optimised servers, now stands at 120GW, with 80% of this capacity in China, the US and the EU. A further 120GW will be built by the end of the decade under the IEA scenario often considered its central base case, of which three-quarters will be AI datacentres.

articles.title: This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
articles.summary: The meeting comes with challenges as there are things Xi does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summit
ByLaura Bicker
China correspondent Reporting fromShenzhen
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
Ukraine, the balancing act
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fourth year, to be on the agenda.

This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.
Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, now into its fourth year, has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives

blocks.text: Russia's invasion of Ukraine, now into its fourth year, has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives

The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.
Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.
China's growing nuclear arsenal
Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.
The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.

The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race. The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.
Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.

Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.

blocks.caption: Image caption, China unveiled intercontinental nuclear missiles at a military parade in 2025

blocks.text: China unveiled intercontinental nuclear missiles at a military parade in 2025
This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.
Will everyone stick to the script?
Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish.
Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.
But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.
Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.
There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.
Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.
The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.
So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.
Xi's problems at home
For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes.
But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A job fair in Jiangsu province: China has been battling youth unemployment in a sluggish economy

blocks.text: A job fair in Jiangsu province: China has been battling youth unemployment in a sluggish economy
He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.

A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.

Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.

At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

articles.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
articles.summary:
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds

One in four women around the world has no power of consent if their husband or…

blocks.text: One in four women around the world has no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.

“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.

“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.

He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.

In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.

Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.

Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.

“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

articles.title: Crimean Bridge has been attacked again, Russian official says
articles.summary: The Crimean Bridge has been attacked again, Crimea's Russian-installed governor said. The attack comes as Vladimir Putin prepares to sit down with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping for joint talks in China.

image.caption: The ‌19-kilometer bridge was inaugurated by Vladimir Putin in 20188 [PHOTO: November 16]Image: Airbus/Vertical 52

blocks.text: The Crimean Bridge was attacked for a third time this week, a Russian official said on Thursday.
Traffic had been temporarily suspended, according to Crimea's Russian-installed governor.
"The damage is currently being assessed," Sergei Aksyonov, the governor, said on Telegram, adding that emergency services were at the scene.
The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.
Crimean Bridge attacked for a third time this week
This is the third Ukrainian attack this week targeting the key strategic bridge that is a key symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.
The bridge has played a key role in supplying Russian troops in occupied parts of southern Ukraine since the 2022 Russian invasion, making it a key target for Kyiv.
Steel arch collapses after Ukrainian drone strikes earlier this week
On Tuesday, Ukraine carried out a major attack on the bridge using missiles and drones, destroying the steel arch of the 19-kilometer-long road section of the crossing.
Ukraine's SBU security service had said that the "road span beneath it (the arch) has been completely destroyed."
The latest attack appears to have impacted rail traffic on the bridge, according to German press agency DPA.

The Ukrainian attack came just hours before an unprecedented meeting scheduled between Putin and his US and Chinese counterparts on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.
What the Putin-Xi huddle could mean for their meeting with Trump

articles.title: Elon Musk says record spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
articles.summary: The multi-billionaire also said he was "not Maga", distancing himself from the political movement linked to Trump.

blocks.text: Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO was the campaign's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of the Senate and House, while Texas, Ohio and other states swung away from Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living.
Musk was speaking virtually at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis, Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Democrats have vowed greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the roll out of controversial data centres.
